title: How do you optimize JDBC reads in Spark — `numPartitions` (parallel connections), `partitionColumn`/`lowerBound`/`upperBound` (range-based parallel reads), `fetchsize` (rows per round trip), and supplying a `query` or `dbtable` with pushdown filters — and how does Spark handle JDBC writes (each task opens its own connection, no cross-task transaction; `isolationLevel` applies per connection)?
shortTitle: How do you optimize JDBC reads and writes in Spark

s1_definition.profdef: When Spark reads from a relational database over JDBC, by default it uses a single connection and pulls the whole table through one task, which is slow and does not scale. Optimizing JDBC reads means telling Spark to open multiple parallel connections by specifying a numeric `partitionColumn` with `lowerBound`, `upperBound`, and `numPartitions` so each task reads a disjoint range, tuning `fetchsize` to control how many rows come back per network round trip, and pushing filters and projections into the SQL so the database does the work. On writes, Spark opens one connection per task and inserts in batches, with no single transaction spanning tasks, and `isolationLevel` is applied per connection.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has a huge ledger in a vault, and you send one clerk through a single door to copy every page one at a time; that is the default single-connection read, and it takes all night. Optimizing is like opening several doors at once and sending many clerks, each told "you copy pages one to one million, you copy one to two million", so they work in parallel. The fetchsize is how many pages each clerk carries per trip to avoid walking back for every single page. And when writing new pages back, each clerk has their own door and their own notebook, so there is no single master transaction covering all of them together.
s1_definition.oneliner: Give Spark a numeric partition column with bounds and a partition count to read a database in parallel, tune fetchsize for round trips, push filters into SQL, and remember each write task is its own connection and its own transaction.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When Spark reads from a relational database over JDBC, by default it uses a single connection and pulls the whole table through one task, which is slow and does not scale. Optimizing JDBC reads means telling Spark to open multiple parallel connections by specifying a numeric `partitionColumn` with `lowerBound`, `upperBound`, and `numPartitions` so each task reads a disjoint range, tuning `fetchsize` to control how many rows come back per network round trip, and pushing filters and projections into the SQL so the database does the work. On writes, Spark opens one connection per task and inserts in batches, with no single transaction spanning tasks, and `isolationLevel` is applied per connection.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has a huge ledger in a vault, and you send one clerk through a single door to copy every page one at a time; that is the default single-connection read, and it takes all night. Optimizing is like opening several doors at once and sending many clerks, each told "you copy pages one to one million, you copy one to two million", so they work in parallel. The fetchsize is how many pages each clerk carries per trip to avoid walking back for every single page. And when writing new pages back, each clerk has their own door and their own notebook, so there is no single master transaction covering all of them together.

**One line to remember:** Give Spark a numeric partition column with bounds and a partition count to read a database in parallel, tune fetchsize for round trips, push filters into SQL, and remember each write task is its own connection and its own transaction.

sections.s2_technical:
By default `spark.read.jdbc(url, "trades", props)` uses one connection and one task, so a billion-row table streams through a single executor and the database serves it from one session. To parallelize, you supply four things together: a numeric or date `partitionColumn`, a `lowerBound`, an `upperBound`, and `numPartitions`. Spark then divides the range into that many slices and generates one SQL query per slice with a WHERE clause on the bound column, so for example with bounds one to one million and ten partitions, task one runs roughly `WHERE id >= 1 AND id < 100000`, task two `WHERE id >= 100000 AND id < 200000`, and so on, each on its own connection. The bounds do not filter data; they only decide where the slice boundaries fall, so values outside the bounds still appear, they just land in the first or last partition. Choosing a partition column with an even distribution matters, because a skewed column makes one task do most of the work.

`fetchsize` controls how many rows the JDBC driver pulls per network round trip. The default is often small, like ten, which means huge tables cause enormous numbers of tiny round trips. Setting `fetchsize` to a few thousand, for example `.option("fetchsize", "10000")`, dramatically cuts round-trip overhead, though too large a value raises executor memory use. You also push work into the database by using a subquery instead of a bare table name: `.option("dbtable", "(SELECT trade_id, amount FROM trades WHERE status='SETTLED') t")` selects only the columns and rows you need so the database filters before data crosses the wire, which is projection and predicate pushdown done manually. Note that when you use `partitionColumn`, you pass a plain `dbtable`, and Spark adds the range predicate itself; when you need a custom query you can also use the `query` option in newer Spark.

For writes, Spark's JDBC sink partitions the DataFrame and each task opens its own connection and issues batched inserts, with `batchsize` controlling rows per batch. A critical consequence is that there is no single transaction across all tasks: if the job fails halfway, some partitions may have committed while others have not, so the target can be left partially written unless you design for idempotency, for example writing to a staging table and swapping, or using an upsert. The `isolationLevel` option, such as READ_COMMITTED, applies to each task's own connection, not across the whole job. The `SaveMode` controls table handling: Append adds rows, Overwrite can truncate or drop-and-recreate depending on the truncate option, and you should prefer `truncate=true` with Overwrite to keep the table's schema and grants. A senior-level nuance is to avoid `numPartitions` that is far larger than the database can handle, because each partition is a live connection and you can exhaust the database's connection pool; a common pattern is to coalesce before writing so you do not hammer the database with hundreds of simultaneous writers.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a nightly job reads the entire trades table from the core banking database into Spark for analytics. The first version used a plain single-connection read and took hours, because one task pulled a hundred million rows through one session while the rest of the cluster sat idle. This is exactly the default-single-partition JDBC problem: without a partition column, Spark cannot split the read, so there is no parallelism.

This is exactly how JDBC read optimization helps. By giving Spark a numeric trade id column with a lower bound, an upper bound, and a partition count, Spark issues one ranged query per partition on its own connection, so many executors read disjoint slices in parallel and the read finishes in minutes.

Problem 2 — The job also wrote a summarized result back to a reporting database, and when it failed partway through, the reporting team found a half-written table because Spark had committed some write tasks but not others. This is exactly the no-cross-task-transaction behavior: each write task is its own connection and its own commit, so there is no global rollback.

In this runnable demo, because we should not require a live database, we simulate a JDBC source and sink in memory. A `FakeJdbcTable` holds rows and records every query it receives so we can prove how many ranged queries Spark would issue and how many round trips fetchsize saves. A `JdbcReadPlanner` computes the per-partition WHERE predicates from bounds and partition count. A `JdbcReader` executes those ranged queries in parallel threads, each simulating its own connection, and applies fetchsize to count round trips. A `JdbcWriter` writes partitions on separate connections, each committing independently, and demonstrates a mid-job failure leaving partial data. The demo prints the generated predicates, the parallelism, the round-trip savings from fetchsize, and the partial-write outcome.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
jdbc:
  url: jdbc:postgresql://core-db:5432/bankdb
  read:
    partition-column: trade_id
    lower-bound: 1
    upper-bound: 1000000
    num-partitions: 10
    fetchsize: 10000
  write:
    batchsize: 5000
    isolation-level: READ_COMMITTED
    num-partitions: 4
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a source table of one million trade ids, read bounds of one to one million with ten partitions and a fetchsize of ten thousand, and a write of four hundred thousand summary rows across four tasks that fails at the third task.

Step 1: The read planner divides the range one to one million into ten slices of a hundred thousand each and builds a WHERE predicate per slice. The first slice uses minus infinity as its lower edge so any ids below the lower bound still get read, and the last slice uses plus infinity so ids above the upper bound are not lost.

Step 2: The reader submits ten tasks to a thread pool, each simulating its own database connection and running its own ranged query. They execute in parallel, so the source table records ten separate queries rather than one, which is the parallelism a single-connection read lacks.

Step 3: Each task pulls its roughly hundred thousand rows in batches of ten thousand because of the fetchsize, so each task makes about ten round trips. Across ten tasks the total round trips are modest.

Step 4: The demo repeats the read with a fetchsize of ten. Now each task needs about ten thousand round trips, and the total balloons, which shows how a small fetchsize cripples throughput even with parallelism.

Step 5: The writer splits four hundred thousand rows across four tasks of a hundred thousand each. Task zero opens its own connection and commits its batches, task one does the same, and then task two throws a simulated failure.

Step 6: Because each task is its own connection and its own transaction, the two hundred thousand rows already committed by tasks zero and one stay in the target even though the job as a whole failed. The log reports the partial write and the absence of a global rollback, which is the behavior you must design around with staging tables or idempotent upserts.

Final output:

```
Oct 30, 2026 7:18:44 AM com.bank.jdbc.JdbcReadPlanner planRanges
INFO: Partition 0: WHERE trade_id >= -9223372036854775808 AND trade_id < 100001
INFO: Partition 9: WHERE trade_id >= 900001 AND trade_id < 9223372036854775807
INFO: Parallel read done: 1000000 rows over 10 connections, 100 round trips (fetchsize=10000)
INFO: Database saw 10 parallel ranged queries (vs 1 for a single-connection read)
WARNING: With fetchsize=10 the same read took 100000 round trips
SEVERE: Write task 2 FAILED — earlier tasks already COMMITTED (no global rollback)
SEVERE: Job failed. Target already has 200000 rows committed by tasks 0 and 1 — partial write, no rollback
```

```
  ┌──────────────────┐     10 ranged SELECTs      ┌──────────────────┐

  Guardrails:
   - numPartitions ≤ DB max connections (avoid pool exhaustion)
   - read from a REPLICA, not the OLTP primary, to protect production
   - writes: staging table + atomic swap OR upsert for idempotency (no global txn)
   - fetchsize tuned (thousands) to cut round trips
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — JDBC Tuning Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Strategy: JdbcReadPlanner computes partitioning strategy          │
  │  Template-ish: JdbcReader runs one ranged query per connection     │
  │     WHY: parallelism = numPartitions independent connections       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Planner plans, Reader reads, Writer writes — one job each      │
  │  O: new partition strategy (hash buckets) = new planner, same rdr  │
  │  D: Reader/Writer depend on FakeJdbcTable abstraction of the DB    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐
  │ JdbcReadPlanner  │─────▶│ JdbcReader       │
  │ + planRanges()   │ gives│ + readParallel() │ ◇ uses FakeJdbcTable
  └──────────────────┘ ranges└─────────────────┘
                              ┌──────────────────┐
                              │ JdbcWriter       │ ◇ uses FakeJdbcTable
                              │ + writePartitioned()│ per-task connection
                              └──────────────────┘

  Contract for readParallel:
    Pre:  ranges cover (-inf, +inf), numPartitions = ranges.size()
    Post: all rows read exactly once across parallel connections
    Tuning: fetchsize = rows per round trip (bigger = fewer trips, more memory)

  Contract for writePartitioned:
    Pre:  DataFrame coalesced to a sane partition count
    Post: each task commits independently; NO cross-task atomicity
    Failure: partial data remains → use staging+swap or upsert

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. JdbcReadPlanner.planRanges("trade_id",1,1_000_000,10) → 10 ranges
  2. JdbcReader.readParallel(ranges, 10000) → 10 parallel SELECTs
  3. (compare) readParallel(ranges, 10) → 100000 round trips (bad)
  4. JdbcWriter.writePartitioned(400000,4,5000, failAt=2)
  5.   task0 commit, task1 commit, task2 FAIL
  6.   200000 rows remain committed → partial write
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
By default Spark reads a JDBC source through a single connection and a single task, which does not scale, so the first optimization is to read in parallel. You give Spark a numeric or date partition column together with a lower bound, an upper bound, and a number of partitions, and Spark divides that range into slices and issues one query per slice with a WHERE clause on the bound column, each on its own connection. The bounds do not filter the data, they only place the slice boundaries, so values outside the bounds still land in the first or last partition, and the partition column should be evenly distributed so one task does not do all the work. Alongside that you tune fetchsize, which is how many rows the driver pulls per network round trip, because the default is tiny and causes huge numbers of round trips on large tables, and you push filters and column selection into the SQL by using a subquery as the dbtable so the database filters before data crosses the wire.

On the write side the behavior is important to understand. Spark partitions the DataFrame and each task opens its own connection and commits its own batches, with batchsize controlling rows per batch. There is no single transaction spanning all tasks, so if the job fails halfway some partitions have already committed while others have not, leaving the target partially written, and the isolation level option applies per connection, not across the job. Because of this I design writes for idempotency, typically writing to a staging table and swapping it in atomically, or using an upsert, and I coalesce before writing so I do not open more connections than the database pool can handle.

At the National Bank of India I used exactly this. A nightly analytics job read the hundred-million-row trades table and the single-connection version ran for hours, so I set a numeric trade id as the partition column with bounds and ten partitions, raised fetchsize to ten thousand, and pointed the read at a read replica rather than the production primary, which brought the read down to minutes. On the write back to the reporting database, a mid-job failure once left a half-written table, and the fix was to write to a staging table and swap it in, which gave me atomic-looking results even though Spark itself offers no cross-task transaction. Those are the levers I reach for: a well-chosen partition column with bounds and partition count for read parallelism, fetchsize and pushdown for throughput, and staging-plus-swap or upsert plus a bounded connection count for safe, idempotent writes.
